title: Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire
intro: The adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire (AdEx) neuron adds one slow adaptation current to the exponential integrate-and-fire neuron. With two variables and about nine parameters it reproduces most firing patterns of cortical neurons and predicts spike times of real cells well.

blocks.source:
C dV/dt   = -g_L (V - E_L) + g_L Delta_T exp((V - V_T) / Delta_T) - w + I
tau_w dw/dt = a (V - E_L) - w

if V >= V_peak:   V <- V_r;   w <- w + b

blocks.text: The first line is the EIF (#/snn/neuron-models/eif) with an extra outward current w. The second line makes w a slow variable with two ways to grow. Subthreshold adaptation, a: w tracks the voltage, like a slow potassium conductance that opens with depolarization. Spike-triggered adaptation, b: every spike adds a fixed jump to w, like calcium-activated potassium currents. Because w subtracts from the input, a neuron that has been firing becomes harder to drive.

items: C, g_L, E_L, V_T, Delta_T: the EIF membrane (Brette-Gerstner values: 281 pF, 30 nS, -70.6 mV, -50.4 mV, 2 mV).
a (nS): subthreshold coupling. Positive a gives adaptation and, together with tau_w, can make the neuron resonate; negative a can produce bistability and rebound firing.
b (pA): spike-triggered jump. Large b gives strong spike-frequency adaptation; b = 0 removes it.
tau_w (ms): how long adaptation lasts, typically 30-300 ms. It sets how quickly the rate settles after a step.
V_r: reset. A reset close to threshold, combined with adaptation, produces bursting: the neuron fires a few quick spikes until w builds up, then pauses.

blocks.text: Naud, Marcille, Clopath and Gerstner (2008) mapped the AdEx parameter space and found these patterns, matching electrophysiology classifications:

items: Tonic spiking: little adaptation (small a and b).
Adapting: large b; the interspike interval lengthens to a steady value. This is typical of regular-spiking pyramidal cells.
Initial burst: reset high and moderate b; a few rapid spikes, then regular firing.
Regular bursting: high reset with large b and long tau_w.
Delayed spiking and transient spiking: negative a or strong subthreshold adaptation.
Irregular firing: near the boundary between patterns, chaotic spike trains appear even without noise.

blocks.text: The defaults are Brette and Gerstner's values; the second series is w divided by 10 so it fits the same axis. Watch the interspike intervals grow as w climbs to a plateau. Set b to 0 and a to 0 to recover the EIF. Raise the reset to about -48 mV with b around 100 pA to get bursts. Raise tau_w to stretch out the adaptation.
Use a step of 0.05-0.1 ms. The exponent is clipped so the upstroke cannot overflow before the peak check catches it.

items: Predictive: adaptive integrate-and-fire models fitted to cortical neurons predict a large fraction of their spike times under fluctuating current (see the Jolivet et al. benchmark below).
Hardware: AdEx is implemented in analog circuits on the BrainScaleS neuromorphic system.
Theory: with a = 0 the subthreshold dynamics stay one-dimensional, so many LIF results carry over.

blocks.text: For a cortical column: AdEx is a strong default for excitatory cells once a LIF prototype works. Adaptation does real computational work in a column. It stops one minicolumn from winning forever, gives a form of short-term memory over the tau_w window, and supports slow, sequence-driven dynamics (#/neuroscience/cortical-columns/temporal-memory). Use adapting parameters for layer 2/3 and layer 4 pyramidal cells, bursting parameters for layer 5, and a = b = 0 for fast-spiking interneurons.

Sources: Brette & Gerstner, "Adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model as an effective description of neuronal activity" (Journal of Neurophysiology, 94, 2005); Naud, Marcille, Clopath & Gerstner, "Firing patterns in the adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model" (Biological Cybernetics, 2008); Jolivet et al., "A benchmark test for a quantitative assessment of simple neuron models" (Journal of Neuroscience Methods, 2008); Gerstner, Kistler, Naud & Paninski, Neuronal Dynamics (Cambridge University Press, 2014), chapter 6.
